newsitem.title: UK: "Sin bins" may make athletes more aggressive - study.
newsitem.headline: "Sin bins" may make athletes more aggressive - study.

text.p: Putting angry ice hockey players into "sin bins" to cool off may just make them more hot-headed, psychologists reported on Tuesday.

They said people tended to mix up the breathlessness caused by exercise with strong emotional responses to anger or elation. This could help explain the "runner's high" but also highlighted the dangers of upsetting an athlete.
Sandy Wolfson and Michael Turnbull of the University of Northumbria tested 27 volunteers by making them exercise at the same time as they solved a simple numbers puzzle.
After about five minutes of rest, they were told they had come first, second or third on the test as compared to other volunteers. A "control" group did not exercise.
"If people had exercised and then told they had come in first place, they were absolutely ecstatic," Wolfson said.
"The control people, if they had been given the good news, they still felt pretty good but not nearly as good as the people in the exercise condition," she added.
But those told they came in last place were in a much worse mood than non-exercisers who were told they had flunked.
"The people who had exercised experienced a much more intense reaction," Wolfson said.

Wolfson told the annual meeting of the British Psychological Society that they had been testing a well-known psychological theory. "People really aren't very good at interpreting their emotions from their physical state," she said.
The problem was that exercise produced some of the same symptoms as emotional arousal -- heavy breathing, raised heartrate and perspiring.
"If people exercise for any period of time and then stop... wait around a little while, what happens is they get a little bit confused about the state of their body," Wolfson said.
"Then when they get some bad news, they mistakenly think that the reason their body is aroused is the new information instead of the exercise."
Wolfson and Turnbull used a widely recognised questionnaire known as the profile of mood state to assess the volunteers' state of mind before and after the exercise.
Wolfson said the effect was widely seen.

"Say you have been to a disco and you have been dancing a lot. Then you meet someone who you find somewhat attractive. According to this theory, you are going to over-react to that person's attractiveness."
That is why she was worried about the "punishment box" in hockey, where players who break the rules are sent to cool off.
"It might have the opposite effect. They are going to be absolutely primed to aggress again," she said.
But she said the effect usually wore off after 15 minutes, when people completely cooled down physically.
